title: Valuation in Four Lessons | Aswath Damodaran | Talks at Google
description:
The tools and practice of valuation is intimidating to most laymen, who assume that they do not have the skills and the capability to value companies. In this talk, I propose to lay out four simple propositions about valuation. The first is that valuation is not an extension of accounting, insofar as it is not about recording the past but forecasting the future. The second is that valuation is not just modeling, where people put numbers into Excel spreadsheets and pump out values. A good valuation requires a narrative that binds the numbers together. The third is that valuing an asset or business is very different from pricing that asset or business, a difference that is often blurred in practice. The fourth is that luck plays a disproportionate role in whether you make money off your valuations. Put differently, you can do everything right and still walk away with nothing or worse at the end.

About the Author
I view myself, first and foremost, as a teacher. I do teach valuation and corporate finance not only to MBAs at Stern but to anyone who will listen (on iTunes U, online and on YouTube). I love to write books, teaching material and blog posts. After 30 years of teaching finance, I still find it fascinating as an interplay of economics, psychology and number crunching.
summary: The talk argues that valuation requires focused research rather than broad searches, noting that some companies like 3M are easy to value due to their mature models while others like Uber and Facebook require specific narratives to justify their prices. The speaker suggests that market momentum can drive valuations higher, as seen with Uber's potential move to $75 billion, while also cautioning that many social media companies operate without immediate profitability. Ultimately, the core argument is that an investor must understand the specific story and user metrics driving a company's worth, such as Facebook's per-user valuation, rather than relying on general market trends.

claims.claim: The speaker expects Tesla to show negative cash flows in the near term as it invests heavily to build assembly plants required for future growth.
claims.quote: So if I'm valuing a Tesla, I should expect to see negative cash flows up front. Why? Because you've got to build those assembly plants to deliver those 10 times more cars I expect you to sell five years from now.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DOMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker uses Uber as an example of a company requiring focused searches rather than broad Google searches when gathering information for valuation.
claims.quote: For instance, I have to value Uber. If I type in Uber in Google, you know what I get? Everything ever said about Google on the face of the Earth. When you search, you want focused searches.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DOMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker describes a valuation of 3M as easy to perform because the company has a long history and a mature business model with little uncertainty about the future story.
claims.quote: So it's a mature company, in what I thought was a mature market. In hindsight, I was hopelessly wrong. But my point is, in valuing 3M, I had to make estimates. But those estimates were easy to make.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DOMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker notes that his blog for posting Apple valuations is hosted on Google, implying a relationship between the two platforms.
claims.quote: on my blog-- which is a Google blog, so that a good think about it-- I post my valuation of Apple, because I don't believe in hype
claims.speaker: ASWATH DOMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker notes that people ask him to explain Uber's $41 billion valuation, but he does not feel the urge to explain what other people pay.
claims.quote: So I get calls saying, how do you explain Uber's $41 billion. Ask somebody who paid the $41 billion. I didn't do it. I just take Uber once in awhile.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DOMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker suggests Uber could be right to aim for a $75 billion valuation if market momentum continues.
claims.quote: If you ask me to explain why people are paying $41 billion for Uber, you know why? Because they think they can sell for $75 billion. That's basically it-- that they think that they can take it in a public offering for $75 billion.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DOMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker estimates Facebook's value at $175 billion based on 1.75 billion users multiplied by a market price of $100 per user.
claims.quote: Facebook is 175 billion users, million users. They wish they had 175 billion. What planets are you going onto? 1.75 billion users-- you multiply that by 100. You get $175 billion.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DOMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker compares the social media valuation model to buying a house, noting that most social media companies make no money.
claims.quote: It's not because how much they made in revenues. It's not because how much money they make. Thank god for that, because most of them make no money.
claims.speaker: ASWATH DOMODARAN

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Uber's valuation ranges from $800 million to $95 billion depending on the narrative used.
claims.quote: At the end of the process, say, based on your story, this is Uber's value. And the value for Uber ranges anywhere from $800 million to $95 billion, depending on the story you tell.
claims.speaker: Aswath Damodaran

claims.claim: The speaker states that the narrative about Google, not exchange rate movements, drives its valuation.
claims.quote: What is the narrative I'm telling about this company? What do I see this company doing? Because that's what's going to drive the valuation of Google, not the fact that because of exchange rate movements, you did not deliver the growth.
claims.speaker: Aswath Damodaran

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that in the case of Apple, the price did move towards the estimated value.
claims.quote: In the case of Apple, it turned out that it did. But it's a sample of one. So it's almost an article of faith.
claims.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
